### page_1
Palaeomagnetism of igneous rocks of the Lake District
(Caledonian) terrane, northern England: Palaeozoic motions
and deformation at a leading edge of Avalonia
J. D. A. PIPER
Geomagnetism Laboratory, Department of Earth Sciences, University of Liverpool, Liverpool L69 7ZE, UK
The Lake District terrane of northern England comprises Upper Cambrian–Silurian sediments and volcanics
accumulated at the northern margin of the Avalonian Plate during growth and demise of the Iapetus Ocean. Ocean
closure and suturing resulted in Late Ordovician and Acadian tectonism and were accompanied by emplacement of a
large regional batholith. Palaeomagnetic study of intrusive igneous rocks, including application of thermal demagnet-
ization, ﬁeld tests and principal component analysis, identiﬁes a history of Ordovician to Devonian magnetization. Late
plutons (Shap and Skiddaw granites and/or aureoles) record a shallow dipolar (A3) axis (mean declination/inclination
(D=I 278= 178) dating from emplacement in late Early Devonian times ( c. 395 Ma). Although this axis is recorded
as a sporadic overprint in older rocks, no pervasive remagnetization is attributable to batholith emplacement. Instead,
the Carrock Fell Complex Layered Gabbros have a mid- to late Ordovician (A1) remanence ( D=I 174=ÿ 5818,
36 samples, a95  488) predating regional F2 folding. Later events in this igneous complex comprise the Carrock Fell
Granophyre with a post-folding Ordovician remanence, and Round Knott Dolerite with a remanence linked to
hydrothermal alteration late in the Ordovician magmatic episode. A Late Ordovician (Ashgill) palaeoﬁeld is also deﬁned
by remanence (A2) in the Threlkeld–St John’s Microgranite and aureole (438 Ma, D=I 2365=6338, 41 samples,
a95  478). Other intrusions carrying a remanence predating the Acadian deformation include the Great Cockup
Picrite (458 Ma, D=I 432=ÿ 3188, 31 samples, a95  778) and basic intrusives in the aureole of the Eskdale
Granite (429 Ma, D=I 1745=2588, 32 samples, a95  888).
Collectively the palaeomagnetic data from this terrane identify a hairpin in the apparent polar wander path during
Late Ordovician (Caradoc–Ashgill) times corresponding to ‘soft’ closure of the Iapetus suture and accompanying
deformation. The same motion is recognized in contemporaneous data from the Welsh Caledonides where declinations
are rotated by c.5 5 8 relative to contemporaneous results from the Lake District. Adjustment for this (probable late
Acadian) rotation beings fold trends of the Paratectonic Caledonides into alignment and identiﬁes a parallel mid- to late
Ordovician destructive plate margin comprising forearc (Lake District) and backarc (North Wales). This arc was
oriented latitudinally in mid-southerly latitudes during formation and the bulk of the magmatism occurred during a
single normal-polarity chron. The relationships between magnetization and folding in both the Lake District and Welsh
Borderlands identify the importance of Late Ordovician deformation along this arc during collision of Avalonia and
Laurentia. Arc-related volcanism was succeeded in Silurian times by parallel foreland basins embracing the Welsh Basin
and southern Lake District as the Laurentian Plate overrode the Avalonian Plate. # 1997 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

KEY WORDS palaeomagnetism; Palaeozoic; Caledonides; Lake District; northern England
1. INTRODUCTION
Assembly of the supercontinent of Pangaea in Palaeozoic times involved collisional docking of large
continental blocks with a long Precambrian history (Gondwana, Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia) plus a
number of smaller continental blocks, mostly with more limited Late Precambrian histories, such as those
now forming the European Massifs. The latter include the Western Avalonian Plate (now sited at the eastern
margin of North America), the Eastern Avalonian Plate including the basement of southern Britain, the
CCC 0072–1050/97/030211–36$17 .50 # 1997 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.
GEOLOGICAL JOURNAL, VOL. 32, 211–246 (1997)

### page_2
Armorican Massif of Brittany and the Bohemian Massif of central Europe. The former continuity between
these terranes is a subject of topical debate but faunal evidence has tended to assign them to a peri-
Gondwanic location in early Palaeozoic times (Cocks and Fortey, 1990; Scotese and McKerrow, 1990)
broadly compatible with high southerly palaeolatitudes in early Ordovician times (Van der Voo, 1993).
The Early Palaeozoic motions between Eastern Avalonia and Laurentia document progressive closure of
the Iapetus Ocean between these blocks (Scotese and McKerrow, 1990), culminating in a ‘soft’collision by
early Silurian times and ﬁnal welding during the Acadian Episode of the Caledonian Orogeny in Late
Silurian–Early Devonian times (Cocks and Fortey, 1990). Volcanic products of Ordovician ocean closure
emplaced above a southerly dipping subduction zone (Fitton and Hughes, 1970) are well represented in
southern Britain and have been the focus of recent palaeomagnetic studies (see summaries in Trench and
Torsvik (1991) and Channell et al. (1992a)). The results form the present basis for correlating Eastern
Avalonia with the larger blocks and document the history of ocean closure and progressive collisionsal
docking that led to formation of Pangaea.
The two major outcrops of Eastern Avalonia comprise the Lake District of northern England and most of
Wales (referred to hereafter as the Welsh Basin). Although palaeomagnetic results from these two terranes
have hitherto been considered as a single entity (Trench and Torsvik, 1991), the regions between (and most of
the remainder of the Eastern Avalonian Block) are widely covered by post-Caledonian sedimentary
successions; hence their tectonic continuity in pre-Acadian times requires evaluation. Furthermore, there are
major gaps in the present data especially during the critical interval of mid-to-late Ordovician times when
faunal evidence suggests that ocean closure was complete and subduction had e ectively ceased.
These problems can be addressed by study of the intrusive igneous rocks spanning these times in both
regions. A study of such rocks in the Lake District inlier is the subject of this paper. Although the age and
tectonic constraints on such bodies are not as precise as controls on the stratiﬁed rocks, which will therefore
more often form the anchor points in any apparent polar wander (APW) path, it is found here that data from
the intrusions widely support the key data; they also serve to document APW during intervals unrepresented
by suitable stratiﬁed formations. In Section 5 the data are compared with contemporaneous results from the
Welsh Basin (Channell et al., 1992a; Piper, 1995) to document kinematic history of the Avalonian Plate
during closure of the Iapetus Ocean and concomitant Caledonian tectonism.
2. GEOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK
The Lake District terrane is the northernmost outcrop linked to the Avalonian Plate in Britain. It is located
immediately south of the Solway Line (Figure 1B) along which Eastern Avalonia merged with Laurentia.
Immediately to the north, a thick prism of Lower Palaeozoic sediments with ophiolitic components was
accreted during a complex history of oblique impingement onto the Laurentian margin and now forms the
Southern Uplands terrane (Bluck, 1985).
During Late Cambrian and Early Ordovician times this margin of Eastern Avalonia was a site of marine
sedimentation. The oldest exposed rocks are the Skiddaw Group comprising 45000 m of graptolitic
mudstones, greywackes and sandstones. Deposition ceased during the D. biﬁdus Biozone of Upper Llanvirn
times (Downie and Soper, 1972; Wadge, 1978). A subsequent volcanic episode in Middle to Late Ordovician
times produced up to 2500 m of basalt and andesite lavas which now form a northern outcrop of Ordovician
volcanics in the Lake District (Eastwood et al., 1968; Figure 1) assigned to the Eycott Volcanic Group
(EVG). Emplacement of the Carrock Fell Layered Gabbro Complex and a variety of smaller intrusions
included in this study (Figure 1 and Table 1) was broadly contemporaneous with this event.
At about the same time, c. 7000 m of volcanics constituting the Borrowdale Volcanic Group (BVG) were
extruded in the central Lake District during a volcanic episode incorporating piecemeal collapse of calderas
(Branney and Soper, 1988), and completed by Early to Middle Caradoc times (D. multidens Biozone
(Wadge, 1978)). This stratigraphic age is supported by a 457+ 4 Ma Sm–Nd mineral age (Thirlwall and

### page_4
Fitton, 1983). The BVG and EVG events (Table 1) have a chemistry compatible with a relatively evolved
continental margin environment (Fitton and Hughes, 1970; Millward et al., 1978). Together with associated
intrusives, they record the ﬁnal phase of subduction-related magmatism at this margin of Avalonia.
Following cessation of volcanism, a transgressing sea deposited limestones, shales, mudstones and
greywackes between Late Caradoc and Ludlow times. This succession forms the Winderemere Supergroup
and makes up the Silurian outcrop in Figure 1. During burial and subsequent Acadian deformation the
Lower Palaeozoic rocks of the Lake District were metamorphosed to no higher than lower greenschist grade,
in common with the paratectonic Caledonides of Wales; this was insucient to comprehensively remagnetize
pre-Acadian rocks which are reported widely to retain an Ordovician remanence record (Briden and Morris,
1973; Piper et al., 1978; Piper, 1979; Channell and McCabe, 1992).
In addition to the basic plutonism noted above, acidic magmatism occurred at various stages between the
intense mid-Ordovician volcanic events and the culmination of tectonic activity in the Acadian episode. A
general distinction is recognized between earlier Na-rich activity and later more K-rich activity (Piper et al.,
1978). The Carrock Fell and Ennerdale Granophyres are typical sub-volcanic plutons, whilst the Threlkeld–
St John’sbody is a microgranite with small phenocrysts of plagioclase and pyroxene suggesting near-liquidus
compositions (O’Brien et al., 1985). The Eskdale, Skiddaw and Shap plutons are coarser-grained bodies
incorporating at least two stages of crystallization and more abundant K-feldspar and quartz.
The regional Bouguer gravity anomaly highlights a large granite batholith underlying much of the Lake
District (Bott, 1974; Lee, 1984), which comes to the surface as the Eskdale Granite in the western Lake
District (Figure 1). Elsewhere it lies at shallow depths with additional cupolas recorded by late plutons (Shap
and Skiddaw) where only roof zones are exposed (Figure 1A). Whilst the gravity expression is comparable to
that of the buried Weardale (410 +10 Ma) and Wensleydale (400 + 10 Ma) granites beneath the Pennines of
central Britain and suggests an Early Devonian origin, the Lake District Batholith has a complex history at
outcrop (Firman, 1978) and emplacement probably spanned the interval between mid-Ordovician and Early
Devonian times: most or all of the granophyres are genetically linked to the volcanic episode whereas the
Shap and Skiddaw Granites are of late Early Devonian age and post-date all but the last and most brittle
deformation (Shepherd et al., 1976; Wadge et al., 1978).
3. FIELD AND LABORATORY METHODS
3a. Strategy of investigation and previous studies
The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely
recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks
(O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting
by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar
assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap
and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the
Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre
is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement.
Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian
thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding
linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian
times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times.
The Carrock Fell Complex was the subject of earlier study employing a.f. demagnetization and endpoint
analysis (Briden and Morris, 1973; Morris, 1973). Since the complex was then considered to be a post-tectonic
event, the data were evaluated in situ; more recent evidence shows that the layered gabbros predate F2 folding
(Roberts, 1971; Harris and Dagger, 1987). The present study includes resampling and stepwise thermal
demagnetization of the Carrock Fell Gabbros and contacts, with fabric also investigated using anisotropy of

### page_5
magnetic susceptibility (AMS), and study of the later stages of magmatism (Carrock Fell Granophyre,
Round Knott Dolerite and cross-cutting dyke swarm). Wider expressions of the mid-Ordovician magmatism
to the west, including the Great Cockup Picrite, are also included in this investigation.
Palaeomagnetic study of the Lake District inlier by Morris (1973) and Briden and Morris (1973) on the
EVG and Carrock Fell Complex was extended to the BVG outcrop of the central Lake District by Faller et al.
(1977) and Piper (1979). More recent investigations employing reﬁned demagnetization and analysis
accompanied by palaeomagnetic ﬁeld tests have focused on the BVG and recognize variable degrees of
partial overprinting (Channell and McCabe, 1992; Piper et al., 1997).
No systematic study has previously been undertaken of the widespread intrusive igneous bodies, although
results from a number of isolated studies are given by Morris (1973) and Piper et al. (1978). They have not
been considered as priorities for palaeomagnetic study owing to age and orientation uncertainties. These
latter are, however, mostly small and the intrusions are therefore targets for investigation because suitable
stratigraphic units are so few (and essentially limited to the EVG and BVG). The intrusions tend to be
magnetically less stable than equivalent volcanics (Morris, 1973; Piper et al., 1978, the Carrock Fell Layered
Gabbros are a notable exception) probably because they are more commonly dominated by larger magnetite
grain sizes and multi domains. Higher failure rates therefore accompany these studies and some samples have
a remanence dominated by Recent ﬁeld components. Nevertheless, numerous intrusive igneous samples
show a coherent remanence structure unobscured by Variscan or later overprinting and it is with these
components that the present study is primarily concerned.
The palaeomagnetic samples were collected in the ﬁeld typically over several metres of outcrop (located in
the data tables by their National Grid reference numbers) using portable drills. Cores were oriented in situ
using Sun and magnetic compasses and cut into 2.4 cm length cylinders for palaeomagnetic processing.
3b. Laboratory methods
Natural remanent magnetizations (NRMs) were measured with ‘Minispin’or SQUID magnetometers and
thermally demagnetized in steps of 50 or 1008C to 5008C; subsequent treatment continued in steps of 15 or
208C to 5808C (or 6808C if haematite carriers were evident). The whole procedure is conducted within sets of
large Rubens coils in which the ambient magnetic ﬁeld is continuously nulliﬁed to minimize secondary
remanence acquisition. Components of magnetization comprising the NRM were recognized by study of
orthogonal projections derived from results of the progressive thermal treatment. Characteristic magnet-
izations (ChRMs) are isolated and directions of components deﬁned by three or more successive steps of
demagnetization determined using principal component analysis.
Ancillary rock magnetic investigations included study of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS)
conducted on selected samples from the Skiddaw Slates, Carrock Fell Layered Gabbros and the Round
Knott Dolerite, and thermomagnetic determinations (saturation remanence, Js , versus temperature deter-
mined with an automated Curie balance) on representative samples of each facies to help identify magnetic
mineral constituents.
4. PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS
4a. The Shap Granite
This ‘granite’is a pink porphyritic adamellite emplaced at the eastern margin of the Lake District inlier
(Figure 1) into Borrowdale Volcanics and Silurian mudstones; the latter were deformed during the Acadian
episode prior to granite intrusion. The pluton is a steep-sided body with a 5 km2 outcrop (Locke and Brown,
1978). Emplacement is well constrained in stratigraphic terms: the youngest invaded country rocks are
deformed sediments of Ludlow age; pebbles of granite found in nearby Lower Carboniferous sediments
identify uplift and unrooﬁng during Devonian times following the Acadian episode.

### page_6
Biotite in the contact aureole has grown along a regional Acadian cleavage but predates a late sub-
horizontal crenulation cleavage (Boulter and Soper, 1973). The structural evidence thus deﬁnes an emplace-
ment which is essentially post-tectonic to the Acadian Episode and has an older limit, of early Gedinnian age
(early Early Devonian (Wadge et al., 1978)). The granite is dated 397+ 7 Ma (mean of K–Ar determin-
ations on biotite) and 394 +3 Ma (Rb–Sr isochron (Wadge et al., 1978)); these ages are conﬁrmed by U–Pb
data from zircons yielding an age of 390+ 7 Ma (Pidgeon and Aftalion, 1978), indicating emplacement
shortly before the Early–Middle Devonian boundary at c. 386 Ma (Harland et al., 1990).
Palaeomagnetic studies on 207 cores from 10 sites distributed at large fresh quarry faces in the pluton
(Figure 2) have been conducted. Approximately equal numbers of cores were drilled from adamellite
intrusion and xenoliths. The xenoliths are BVG lavas and Silurian mudstones variably digested and
recrystallized within the igneous host. Reﬂecting their diverse origins, the xenoliths have a wider range of
intensities of magnetization (4 106–6 103 A m2=kg) than the adamellite (7 106–8 104 A m2=kg) but
are typically more strongly magnetized by an order of magnitude. Thermomagnetic study identiﬁes discrete
magnetite Curie points linked to accessory grains of this mineral. This behaviour is also typical of xenoliths
and the saturating phase undergoes little alteration on heating in air (Figure 3). There is no appreciable
indication of the red haematite pigment in the orthoclase phenocrysts; since the thermomagnetic curves are
dominated by the magnetite this is not unexpected because the saturation remanence of haematite is only
c. 2% of that of magnetite.
Some samples at all locations have dominant steep positive (‘B’)components resident in the magnetite
spectrum (sample 3-13 in Figure 4) which generally do not quite converge on the origin; a small residual
component is evident but not resolved. This higher blocking temperature (h.b.t.) component is recognized in
other samples with little or no B component where it is present as a weaker magnetization of lower stability
with easterly or westerly declination and shallow inclination (samples 1–4 and 8–12 in Figure 4). Thus both

polarities of this (‘A3’)magnetization are recorded. In a few cases (e.g. sample 7-11 in Figure 4) each polarity
appears to be subtracted successively; cooling through the magnetite blocking temperature spectrum has
probably recorded polarity reversal in these examples. Deﬁnition of the A3 component deteriorates as the
relative magnitude of the B component increases; when B dominates the spectrum, A3 is often still
recognizable but vector deﬁnition is erratic. B is unblocked at a wide range of temperatures between 100 and
5008C, whilst A3 is unblocked at temperatures ranging from 400 to 6308C, implying some presence in the
pigmentary haematite.
The distribution of component directions shows slight smearing between the B and westerly A3 groups
(Figure 4) suggesting that they have not always been fully resolved; however, mean directions of the two A3
polarities (calculated for inclination I < 258) are nearly antiparallel. The 95% conﬁdence cones overlap but
the angle between the normal and reversed axes (11.58) is slightly greater than that required for a positive
reversal test (9.68 (McFadden and McElhinny, 1990)). The other feature of the palaeomagnetic record in this

pluton is sporadic preservation, mostly at site 9, of a poorly deﬁned SW component unblocked by
400–5008C (sample 9-2 in Figure 4). This was recognized by earlier a.f. demagnetization of 12 samples from
the same location (Piper et al., 1978) but is evidently not the ChRM in the pluton.
The mean of the B components (declination/inclination D=I 345=728, 54 components, a95  558) is
close to the present magnetic ﬁeld (D=I 355=718) and therefore interpreted to be of Recent viscous origin.
The presence of both polarities in the (predominantly magnetite-resident) A3 magnetization suggests that it
is the ChRM of primary cooling-related origin. This interpretation can potentially be tested in this case by
two palaeomagnetic ﬁeld tests, namely (i) a contact test on the country rocks of the aureole and (ii) a
conglomerate test on overlying Lower Carboniferous conglomerates.
Basaltic lavas belonging to the BVG were sampled in the Shap Blue Quarry and adjoining stream sections
(Figure 2). In these rocks metasomatic inﬂuence of the pluton is shown by development of epidote and other
low-grade minerals. Magnetizations (site 12) are dominated by large lower blocking temperature (l.b.t.)
components apparently acquired in the present ﬁeld and comparable to the B component in the pluton
(Figure 5). A residual convergent magnetite-resident component was recovered in 13 of 17 cores following
subtraction of the B component, with a direction similar to the westerly shallow A3 remanence in the pluton
(Figure 5 and Table 2). This is widely removed from the ChRM in the BVG which is directed NNE (Piper
et al., 1997) (the lavas have low dip at this location); the primary remanence in the lavas therefore appears to
have been completely overprinted by thermal e ects of the pluton.
The aureole also cuts the Stockdale Rhyolite, the last expression of Borrowdale volcanism in the Lake
District; this has been sampled at site 11 (Figure 2). Magnetizations are very weak (c. 10ÿ7 A m2/kg) but
progressive thermal demagnetization above 5008C again isolates similar components to the A3 magnet-
ization recognized in the pluton (Figure 5 and Table 2); in this case examples of both polarities are recorded
with no prominent record of the B magnetization. No vestiges of the primary (steep negative-directed)
remanence found in the rhyolite elsewhere (Piper et al., 1997) are observed; hence this unit has also been
overprinted by thermal inﬂuence of the pluton.

Silurian mudstones (site 13, Figure 2) at the southern margin of the pluton proved to be a less suitable
facies for a contact test. Weak remanence is fully subtracted by 350–4008C and therefore probably resident in
pyrrhotite (Figure 5). Most ChRMs are of reversed polarity but variable direction; they correspond broadly
to the predicted ﬁeld direction in Late Palaeozoic times and include the minor direction recognized in the
pluton. Only two of 17 cores yield an h.b.t. component approximately corresponding to the A3 remanence in
the pluton. Diagenetic mineral growth in the mudstones (possibly during the last stages of cleavage
development in the Acadian Episode (see Boulter and Soper, 1973)) has evidently obscured signiﬁcant record
of overprinting by the igneous body.
Detritus from the Shap Granite occurs in basal conglomerates at Shap Wells (sites 14 and 15 in Figure 2)
deposited during the Dinantian sub-System of Early Carboniferous times. It underlies Chadian-age rocks
and may date from the Courceyan Stage (Garwood, 1913). Material derived from the Shap Granite is in the
form of disaggregated feldspar phenocrysts and could not be reliably sampled for palaeomagnetic study.

However, 30 clasts of tu s, lavas and mudstones derived from the adjoining Lower Palaeozoic outcrop were

Remanence components isolated by thermal demagnetization come from 24 clasts, all in volcanic samples
derived from the adjoining BVG outcrop. Most magnetizations have two-component structures with good
within-clast agreement recognized in the h.b.t. components (samples 5, 13 and 15 in Figure 6); no common
overprint is evident. The group mean from the clast lithologies is random at the 95% conﬁdence level
(Table 2) and only two clasts (15A, 16) include directions similar to the axis recognized in the underlying
pluton; whilst most clasts exhibit dual-component behaviours, in no case is the component structure similar
to the remanence in the adamellite or to the comparable BVG lithologies in th aureole. Hence the test implies
that remanence isolated from the pluton predates deposition of the conglomerate in Early Carboniferous
times.

4b. The Skiddaw Granite aureole
The Skiddaw Granite is another member of the post-orogenic granite suite. It was emplaced into deformed
Skiddaw Slates and the Carrock Fell Complex (Figures 1 and 7). Only three small outcrops are exposed in
the ﬂoor of the Caldew Valley but a wide thermal aureole identiﬁes this as the roof zone of a large subcrop
rising from the regional batholith (Eastwood et al., 1968; Figure 1). Illite, developed along regional
cleavage in the country rock slates, is dated 395 Ma by K–Ar (Ineson and Mitchell, 1974), comparable to a

determination on the granite of 397 + 4 Ma (K–Ar on biotite (Shepherd et al., 1976)). The regional Acadian
cleavage a ects strata as young as Downtonian (early Gedinnian) in age; granite emplacement overlapped
this event to produce a comparable relationship between emplacement and late regional cleavage to that seen
in the Shap Granite aureole (Soper and Roberts, 1971). Emplacement ages of the two plutons are thus
indistinguishable. At outcrop the Skiddaw pluton is a coarse-grained leucocratic granite which has su ered
extensive hydrothermal alteration with partial conversion to a greisen; it is therefore unsuitable for
palaeomagnetic study and sampling was concentrated on hornfelsed Skiddaw Slates in the country rock
margin at seven sites (diamond symbols 1–7 in Figure 7).
The anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) is conveniently expressed in terms of a triaxial ellipsoid
with maximum (k1 or kmax), intermediate (k2 or kint) and minimum (k3 or kmin) axes. The Skiddaw hornfels is
derived from a parent Skiddaw Slate but the degree of AMS (k1/k3) is mostly less than 1.15 and probably
reﬂects static recrystallization (Figure 8). A broad girdle of k2 and k3 axes of oblate fabrics in the contact slates
is orientated NNE–SSW with westerly dips (Figure 9); streaking in the k1 directions records the near E–W
strike of the regional F2 fold and exhibits the easterly plunge of this fold structure (Figure 7; Roberts, 1971).
Hence recrystallization to hornfels has been dominated by a fabric inherited from the F2 folding with the
NNE–SSW girdle resulting from refolding and ampliﬁcation of this structure during Acadian and Variscan
Episodes (Section 4g).

Slates in the contact aureole show two types of thermomagnetic spectra (Figure 3). Exponential decrease
in Js is the signature of a dominant paramagnetic component, although some conversion to magnetite takes
place on cooling; biotite and chlorite are important constituents of the slates in the granite aureole
(Eastwood et al., 1968) and are probably responsible for this signature. In the second curve type an inﬂection
at about 3508C indicates breakdown of a ferromagnetic mineral (probably pyrrhotite) with growth of
magnetite identiﬁed on the cooling curves.

typical directions close to the present ﬁeld are attributable to Recent ﬁeld acquisition. The only evidence for a
more ancient component was found in hornfels within a few metres of the granite contact at sites 6 and 7,

### page_16
in the western Lake District (Figure 1). A Rb–Sr determination of 420+ 4 Ma (Rundle, 1979) on the
granophyre is younger than a determination on the Eskdale Granite (429 +4 Ma); it probably reﬂects
problems of dating ﬁne-grained acid igneous rocks by Rb–Sr and is likely to be a minimum estimate (O’Brien
et al., 1985).
The granophyre is primarily an intergrowth of perthite and quartz with only minor amounts of maﬁc
accessories altered to chlorite and epidote. However, small dolerite intrusions are associated with basiﬁed and
hybrid granophyres (Firman, 1978). Although poorly exposed, they are more strongly magnetic than the host
granophyre and can be mapped from ground magnetic surveys. These identify impersistent WNW–ESE
trending anomalies; outcrop was detected and sampled at seven of these anomalies (sites 1-5 and 7 in
Figure 11b plus an additional site (6) near Wastwater Lake to the east). Whilst intrusion ages are uncertain, an
origin related to emplacement with, or soon after, the granophyre is probable because they are not observed in
the younger Eskdale Granite. Site 7 is in basic facies of the granophyre pluton. Site 6 near Wastwater Lake
may have a di erent origin because a dyke-like form is suggested by a long linear outcrop with discrete
contacts.
ChRMs are dominated by components with southerly directions and shallow to intermediate positive
inclination recovered following removal of present ﬁeld components (sample 2-4 in Figure 11a) or a shallow
A3 component (sample 5-5) recording overprinting by the regional batholith (Sections 4a and 4b). The
exception is site 4 (e.g. sample 4-5 in Figure 11a) where single and very stable NNW positive components are
present. The population of southerly directed magnetizations with three antiparallel components (Figure 11c)
has a mean of D=I 175= 268 (Table 4). Aberrant site 4 has a magnetization comparable to the Carrock
dyke swarm in the eastern Lake District (Section 4j).

Since the granophyre is intruded by the large Eskdale Granite pluton which attains the surface near the
southern part of the study area (Figure 1), pre-Eskdale bodies in the granophyre are likely to record a cooling
remanence related to granite emplacement. The Eskdale Granite is dated by Rb–Sr and K–Ar (420 + 4 and
427 +8 Ma (Rundle, 1979)) and is considered to be syntectonic. Tilt adjustments are therefore uncertain but
are unlikely to be appreciable both because the body is part of a large and massive outcrop more than 15 km
N–S in width, and because local tilts of the BVG are small. The Palaeolatitude derived from the in-situ result
(138S) is close to data from late Llandovery sediments in the Howgill Fells immediately to the east of the
Lake District terrane (128S (Channell et al., 1993)) and from mid-Wenlock rocks of Britain close to the
Variscan Front (128S (Torsvik et al., 1993)); this is compatible with the radiometric age of 429 Ma.

4d. The Carrock Fell Complex: the Layered Gabbro Series
The Carrock Fell Complex comprises a Gabbroic Series emplaced along the contact between the Skiddaw
Slates and Eycott Volcanic Group (Figures 1 and 7). It possesses a broad symmetry with iron-ore and
pyroxene/hornblende-rich melagabbros at the margins of the body giving way inwards to banded gabbros
displaying alternate maﬁc and felsic layers, and then to feldspathic leucogabbros which sandwich a central
mesocratic gabbro (Eastwood et al., 1968; Firman, 1978; Bowden and Hunter, 1990; Figure 12). A high-
amplitude magnetic anomaly reﬂects the general strike of the layering in the unexposed vicinity of the contact
with the Carrock Fell Granophyre. None of the exposed gabbro facies are strongly magnetized in a way
which can explain this anomaly (Figure 12) and it is probably caused by buried segregations of pyrrhotite
within the gabbro (also found located near the base of the complex in its westerly extension (see Patrick,
1980)) or by strongly magnetized ferrogabbros.
The igneous banding has steep northerly dips and all workers, until recently, have considered that
emplacement occurred as a sub-vertical body in the present orientation (Harker, 1894; Hollingworth, 1938;
Eastwood et al., 1968; Briden and Morris, 1973). Harris and Dagger (1987), however, evaluated ﬁeld
evidence to show that the layered gabbros were originally emplaced as part of a sub-horizontal tabular body
and folded by the regional F2 deformation. Speciﬁcally, these authors show that the distribution and
orientation of country rock xenoliths is compatible with a former ﬂoor sited at the present southern contact
(Figure 12); rhythmic layering and modal distributions in the banded gabbros support the same conclusion.
K–Ar biotite dates from the Layered Gabbro Series yield a range of ages between 439+ 10 and
468 +10 Ma (Rundle, 1979, 1981), indicating a mid-to Late Ordovician age. Geochemical evidence for a
common tholeiitic fractionation trend (Hunter, 1980; O’Brien et al., 1985; Bowden and Hunter, 1990)
Figure 12. Geological map of the Carrock Fell Complex simpliﬁed after Eastwood et al. (1968), showing the distribution of
palaeomagnetic sampling sites of this study. Also shown are the orientations of AMS ellipsoids in the Layered Gabbro Series and
gabbro hornfels; the arrows point in the k1 direction and the sectors show the orientations of the foliation plane incorporating k1 and k2

See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License

### page_18
supports a correlation with the adjoining EVG and supports the view that the Gabbro Series is part of a sub-
volcanic complex which fed the lavas above (Eastwood et al., 1968).
The Layered Gabbros have weak, typically oblate, AMS fabrics with anisotropy degrees (k1/k3) mostly less
than 1.04 but sometimes higher than 1.10 (Figure 8). The k1 and k2 axes occupy a girdle dipping northwards
at intermediate angles (Figure 9) similar to, but typically slightly less than, the dips of the mineral layering
observed at the eastern margin of the outcrop (50–708N (Eastwood et al., 1968)); k3 axes dip at intermediate
angles to the south, perpendicular to this foliation. Fabric in the magnetic susceptibility therefore
approximately records the primary igneous layering in the body and contrasts with fabric in the adjoining
country rock hornfels (site 12, Figure 12). However, the k1 axes also dip mostly to the north at intermediate
angles (Figure 9) and close to the dip of the F2 fold limb; they therefore identify a relationship with the
regional tectonic history and suggest that lineation has been imparted to the igneous foliation by the F2
deformation (Section 4g). Thermomagnetic spectra in the gabbros are dominated by strong saturation
remanences with Curie points close to that of pure magnetite and little alteration on heating (Figure 3).
The Layered Gabbros of both melanocratic and leucocratic facies have strong and very stable magnet-
izations; single components are isolated above 2008C and dominated by narrow and discrete ChRMs
typically subtracted over 208C or less between 540 and 5608C (e.g. samples 6-1, 8-5 and 10-1 in Figure 13).
The majority of directions have northerly declinations with shallow negative inclinations (mean D=I
357=ÿ 168, Figure 14). The exception is a single site (9) where a majority of cores (e.g. sample 9-4 in
Figure 13) are overprinted by a ﬁeld direction recorded in late dolerite dykes cutting the complex (Section 4j).
The dominance of one magnetite-held component in the remanence structure of the Layered Gabbros
accounts for good agreement between this study and the earlier result derived from a.f. demagnetization and
endpoint analysis (D=I 353=ÿ 188 (Briden and Morris, 1973; Morris, 1973)). Skiddaw Slate at the lower
margin of the complex has been baked to a white hornfels; ﬁve of eight samples from a site (12) within 4 m of
this contact yield discrete magnetite-held components (sample 12-1 in Figure 13) close to the gabbro
remanence. Although blocking-temperature spectra are somewhat lower and more distributed than in the
gabbro, directions are indistinguishable; behaviours contrast with slate in the granite aureole (Section 4b)
and record thermal overprinting by the gabbro complex.
Three episodes of folding (F1–F3) have been recognized in the Skiddaw Slate Group immediately to the
south of the Carrock Fell Complex by Roberts (1971). The Layered Gabbros are in the northern limb of a
large regional-scale F2 fold with ENE–WSW trending axis (Figure 7). Tight upright folds of the F1
generation are only observed in the Skiddaw Slates (Helm and Roberts, 1971; Wadge, 1971) and are now
regarded as soft-sediment deformation. The outcrop of the EVG in Figures 1 and 7 highlights the form of the
F2 structure evident from the 1 : 63 360 geological map of the region (Sheet 23, Cockermouth; Eastwood
et al., 1968) and identiﬁes a plunge to the east (c. 388/868E). It has a composite origin: the late Caledonian
Acadian F3 folding produced E–W-trending open folds (Roberts, 1971) and was probably responsible for
amplifying the F2 structure. In addition, the unconformably overlying Lower Carboniferous rocks dip at
gentle angles (typically 10–158) northwards and eastwards around this margin of the inlier, showing that
Variscan deformation has further enhanced the observed amplitude and plunge. Since successive com-
pressive events were directed approximately N–S, the structure can be treated as a single entity for purposes
of tilt adjustment (Harris and Dagger, 1987).
These latter authors note that adjustment for plunge and residual tilt of the a.f. demagnetized result from
the Carrock Complex (Briden and Morris, 1973) moves the in-situ result (D=I 353=ÿ 188) to a steeper
negative inclination (D=I 315=ÿ 588), more compatible with results from the EVG (D=I 5=ÿ 438) and
the BVG (D=I 341=ÿ 478 and D=I 347=ÿ 628; see discussion in Section 5 and in Briden and Morris
(1973), Faller et al. (1977), Channel and McCabe (1992) and Piper et al., (1997). This correction also bring
poles to the layering in the Gabbro Series near to the vertical (Harris and Dagger, 1987), supporting
emplacement (and magnetization) of the Layered Gabbro Series as a quasi-horizontal sheet.
The AMS data and new palaeomagnetic results permit reﬁnement to this result. The magnetic fabric
deﬁnes a foliation plane dipping to the north with a mean orientation direction of D=I 14=468.

(Signiﬁcant deviation occurs at site 13 near the eastern margin of the complex (Table 5); since this is also

BVG primary magnetizations and the regional Late Ordovician overprint (D=I 347=ÿ 628) on the BVG
and is therefore compatible with magnetization late in the EVG/BVG igneous episode.
4e. The Carrock Fell Complex: the Carrock Granophyre
The Layered Gabbros of the Carrock Fell Complex are intruded by two igneous bodies, the Carrock Fell
Granophyre and the Round Knott Dolerite (Eastwood et al., 1968). The granophyre is a typical sub-volcanic
intrusion emplaced as a steep-sided body cutting the inclined layering of the gabbros. Geochemical data
(Hunter, 1980; O’Brienet al., 1985) relate it to a tholeiitic trend in common with the gabbros and EVG.

4f. The Carrock Fell Complex: the Round Knott Dolerite
This dyke-like body cuts the Layered Gabbros (Figure 12) and attains a maximum thickness of 0.5 km.
Although it appears to divide a once-continuous granophyre body (Figure 12), age relationships between the
dolerite and the Carrock Fell Granophyre are unclear (Eastwood et al., 1968); the dolerite is probably mostly
younger, although any age di erences are likely to be slight because the dolerite is locally veined by
granophyre. It is, however, much more altered than both the Layered Gabbros and Granophyre, and the
younger dolerite dykes, and is referred to as ‘diabase’in the early literature (Harker, 1894). Feldspar is
profoundly sericitized, whilst widespread development of chlorite and secondary amphibole, as well as
peripheral alteration of opaques, are evident in thin section; the dominance of secondary minerals is reﬂected
in a high content of combined water in the chemical analyses (Eastwood et al., 1968).
The dolerite possesses only slight magnetic fabric, with anisotropy degrees mostly c. 1.01–1.02 (Figure 8).
The k1 axes exhibit a weak tendency to lie in the plane of this steep dyke-like intrusion (Figure 9) cutting the
gabbro fabric obliquely and correlating with the ENE–WSW outcrop (Figure 12). Although apparently
related to primary emplacement, this fabric probably records alignment of pseudomorphing secondary

### page_23
minerals such as chlorite because thermomagnetic spectra have a dominant paramagnetic expression
(Figure 3); weak magnetite Curie points are sometimes evident, with conversion to magnetite apparent in the
cooling curves.
In common with earlier observations by Morris (1973) and Briden and Morris (1973), no stable
demagnetization behaviour was recognized close to the intrusive contact with the Skiddaw Granite (sites 1
and 2 in Figure 12). Where strong magnetizations are present they are largely unblocked in the ﬁrst stages of
treatment, mostly below 2008C, and are likely to reside in secondary multidomain carriers grown during
thermal metamorphism. At greater distances from the granite contact components deﬁned by thermal
demagnetization reﬂect the overprinting e ects of the granite and are more prominent in this body than in
the Layered Gabbros or Granophyre (Figure 14). Other samples have a SSW ChRM following removal of
a present ﬁeld component (sample 3-4 in Figure 13). This is magnetite-held like the granite overprints and,
since it is also close to the Early Carboniferous palaeoﬁeld direction, cannot positively be identiﬁed as older
than the granite. However, overprinting of this age is not recognized elsewhere in the region; furthermore
four samples illustrate a reversal in this component (sample 5-5 in Figure 13). The angle between axes deﬁned
by the normal and reversed components is 11.08, which is less than the critical angle of 15.28 and yields a
positive class C reversal test (McFadden and McElhinny, 1990). Thus in addition to partial overprinting by
the Skiddaw Granite, a NNEÿ=SSW axis of magnetization is recognized (Figure 14) with a mean
direction D=I 206=388 (Table 6).
This palaeoﬁeld direction is divergent from magnetizations identiﬁed in the Layered Gabbros and
Granophyre. In view of the profound hydrothermal alteration of the dolerite compared with the other facies
of the igneous complex, it is likely to be younger in age and is probably related to pneumatolitic alteration
during emplacement of the dolerite. Adjustment for tilt of the Layered Gabbros moves the mean to
D=I 267=628; this would imply that the body had a sheet-like form inclined to the north at the time of
magnetization and is clearly inappropriate. Only adjustment for tilt of Carboniferous strata to the east is
therefore applied in Table 6.

4g. The palaeomagnetic record in the Carrock Fell Complex
Application of tilt adjustment implied by the fabric in the gabbro to the Carrock Fell Granophyre moves
the remanence to D=I 193=ÿ 738. The in-situ remanence in the granophyre is therefore signiﬁcantly closer
to that in the dipping Layered Gabbro series after tilt adjustment of the latter (Figure 15); it also then
accords most closely with the palaeoﬁeld directions in the stratiﬁed rocks (EVG and BVG) which are directly
referable to a palaeohorizontal. The palaeomagnetic data therefore imply that the granophyre was emplaced
after formation of the major fold structure; this is also implicit in its near-vertical orientation. A few steeper
NNW- partial l.b.t. overprints in gabbro samples (Figure 14) might record partial overprinting by the
granophyre body, whereas no northerly shallow negative in-situ remanences like those characterizing the
gabbro are observed in the granophyre.
Hence palaeomagnetic evidence identiﬁes the F2 deformation as an event occurring during emplacement
of the Carrock Fell Complex and prior to mid-Caradocian times. Although an end-Silurian (Acadian)
age for this folding has been proposed on the basis of fold trends (Roberts, 1971) and generally accepted
subsequently (Soper and Moseley, 1978), an Upper Ordovician age is supported by several observations:
(i) the near-vertical orientations of the Carrock Fell Granophyre and Round Knott Dolerite bodies;
(ii) the in-situ remanence in the Granophyre is closest to that of the Layered Gabbros after the latter have
been adjusted for tilt; (iii) the AMS fabric in the Layered Gabbros, which is primarily related to igneous
layering, also records the imprint of F2 deformation whilst no vestige of this episode is evident in the Round
Knott Dolerite emplaced late in the igneous cycle (Figure 9); (iv) a pre-Silurian dyke swarm in this region
cuts the Carrock Fell Complex and is probably a late expression of the Ordovician magmatism (Eastwood
et al., 1968); the dykes cut the major F2 fold and have near-vertical orientations (Section 4j); and ﬁnally
(v) outcrop of Drygill Shales (mid-Caradoc, Longvillian) within the igneous complex (Figure 12) is
intruded by felsite and cut by the dykes (Eastwood et al., 1968); this formation was deposited on the eroded
F2 antiform (the shales now occur at a structural level well below the EVG) but was folded prior to dyke
emplacement. These diverse lines of evidence indicate that both magmatism and deformation were concen-
trated in Early to Middle Caradoc times.
The Carrock Fell Granophyre and Round Knott Dolerite remanence directions clearly require adjustment
for deformation of the post-Lower Carboniferous rocks. Since residual e ects of Acadian deformation
cannot be discerned, the palaeomagnetic results from these two bodies are not ﬁrst-rank data. They do,
however, have two important regional implications. (i) Since their in-situ magnetizations correspond most
closely with the EVG, BVG and fully tilt-adjusted Carrock Fell Gabbro results, emplacement at a late stage
in the Middle to Upper Ordovician cycle occurred after the bulk of regional deformation was complete.
(ii) Both granophyre and dolerite record the ﬁrst evidence for reversed polarity in the Ordovician magmatic
activity; hence they place the major phases of Lake District Ordovician magmatism close to a polarity
boundary following the exclusive normal polarity observed in the major phases of magmatic activity (EVG,
BVG, Carrock Gabbros and Great Cockup Picrite, see Section 5a).
4h. The Great Cockup Picrite intrusion, northern Lake District
A suite of intrusions emplaced into the Skiddaw Slate north of Bassenthwaite in the northern Lake
District (Figure 7) is linked by common feldspar and maﬁc compositions, and considered to be a part of a
single consanguinous group (Eastwood et al., 1968). Sample sites 1 and 2 (see Table 7 and Figure 7) are from
separated outcrops in the same (Great Cockup) picrite intrusion (Postlethwaite, 1892) and site 6 is from the
smaller Little Knott Picrite body. The remaining sites are in bodies of dioritic petrography although all have
lamprophyric anities (Eastwood et al., 1968). Three K–Ar hornblende ages on the Great Cockup Picrite
yield an average age of 458 + 9 Ma (Rundle, 1979), with the oldest determination (468 + 10 Ma) identical to
the oldest K–Ar biotite age from the Carrock Fell Gabbro. The dioritic bodies have a geochemistry relating
them to the Eycott Volcanic Group (Firman, 1978); thus the sampled intrusions 1 to 8 in Figure 7 are all
linked to the Carrock–Borrowdale–Eycott igneous episode.

Petrographic examination shows all olivine in the picrite intrusions (sites 1, 2 and 6) to be altered to
serpentine; Ti-augite is also variably altered. Primary compositional zoning and ophitic textures are,
however, preserved and primary hornblende is not visibly altered; this latter mineral contains abundant
opaque inclusions. More acid members including the diorites are more profoundly altered, especially the
c. 100 m thick Embleton sill at site 8, where both hornblende and biotite are partially converted to chlorite;
opaques are in large skeletal aggregates associated with alteration and likely to be secondary. All intrusions
contain secondary quartz whilst the diorites are also extensively veined with carbonate.
These intrusions comprise outcrop near the edge of the Skiddaw Granite aureole (Figure 7) and the only
discernible non-viscous components comprise overprints in a direction comparable to the batholith.
The dominant feature of remanence in the Great Cockup Picrite, however, is a magnetite-resident compo-
nent with NE declination and shallow inclination recovered following removal of a present ﬁeld magnet-
ization or a batholith overprint (samples 1-16 and 2-14 in Figure 17). All samples with this ChRM have the
same polarity (Figure 17) and (excluding probable Skiddaw Granite overprints with D> 708E, the A3
magnetizations in Figure 17) yield a group-mean direction of D=I 427=328 (Table 7).
The only analogous palaeoﬁeld directions are of Upper Palaeozoic age but of opposite polarity (S-SW
shallow) and were acquired during the Permo-Carboniferous reversed superchron; hence the magnetization
in the picrite appears to predate deformation. The pluton is emplaced into folded Skiddaw Slates dipping NE

applicable to both the Great Cockup Picrite and the northern part of the EVG outcrop; hence it is inter-
preted to record polar movement between remanence acquisition of the picrite and the EVG (Section 5b).
4i. The Threlkeld–St John’sMicrogranite
This body is emplaced close to the contact between the Skiddaw Slates and BVG (Figure 1) and exposed as
three small outcrops, two of which have been extensively quarried. The microgranite contains xenoliths of
both Skiddaw Slate and Borrowdale Volcanics (Rastall, 1940), whilst the typical sub-volcanic nature of the
pluton indicates a genetic link with late stages of Borrowdale activity. A Rb–Sr isochron age of 438 +6 Ma
(Wadge et al., 1974; Rundle, 1981), equivalent to a late Ashgill stratigraphic age, also indicates that the
microgranite was emplaced as a late phase of the Ordovician magmatism.
Thermal demagnetization of 116 individually oriented cores distributed over quarry outcrops of the
microgranite and contacts isolates a component structure in weak magnetizations (c. 10ÿ7 A m2/kg) resident
in magnetite. The ChRM component has positive inclination and southerly direction; with the exception of
an l.b.t. component removed in the ﬁrst step of treatment in some samples, it appears to be discrete
(Figure 18a). Samples of Skiddaw Slate within a few metres of the margin of the pluton exhibit a component
with the same direction. A few samples show weak evidence for reversal in the highest part of the spectrum
(e.g. contact slate sample shown in Figure 18b, although only one acceptable component trajectory was
resolved; no coherent components were isolated from slate samples further from the contact.
Sixty-seven samples possessed stable components of non-viscous origin. ChRM directions are pre-
dominantly SSW positive (Figure 18c and Table 8) and this population yields a mean direction of D=I

and, together with the evidence for overprinting at the contact with the slate country rock, suggests a
primary remanence related to igneous cooling.
BVG lavas in the adjoining outcrop to the south have low southerly dips (c. 108/1708E); hence tilt
adjustment shifts the remanence direction only slightly to D=I 2212=5818. The Rb–Sr age implies that the
pluton is c. 20–25 Ma younger than the Carrock Fell Gabbro; it is also predominantly of opposite (reversed)
polarity thus contrasting with the predominant normal polarities of the Carrock Fell Complex, BVG and
EVG. Since the Carrock Fell Complex was being emplaced during regional F2 folding (Section 4g), reman-
ence in the Threlkeld–St John’sbody is likely to post-date Late Ordovician folding. The magnetization is
then equivalent to a palaeolatitude of 458S and a pole position at 3188E, 208N; the declination is rotated by
c. 408 anticlockwise from remanence in the Caradocian rocks and identiﬁes terrane rotation between c. 465
and 440 Ma. Twelve sample components in the pluton with aberrant directions are of shallower inclination
and most have easterly directions (Figure 18c); a correlation with A3 implies a patchy overprinting during
regional batholith emplacement.
4j. Post-Carrock Fell Complex dyke swarms
Dykes of quartz dolerite and ‘porphyrite’composition are emplaced into the Carrock Fell Complex and
adjoining Skiddaw Slates and Eycott Volcanic Group (Eastwood et al., 1968). The spatial relationship to the
complex and absence of high-level intrusion in this region during Silurian times identify them as a late phase
of the Ordovician magmatic activity (no post-Ordovician volcanic activity is identiﬁed in this region with the
exception of a thin suite of basaltic lavas at the base of the Carboniferous succession at the western margin of
the outcrop in Figure 7 (Oppenheim et al., 1993)). Trends range from ESE–WNW to E–W (mostly within
the Carrock Fell Complex) to ENE–WSW.
Four of ﬁve sampled dykes cutting the Eycott Volcanic Group at Eycott Hill (sites 1–4 in Figure 7 and see
dyke sample in Figure 13) have NE–SW trends and yield discrete NE-directed ChRMs with negative inclin-
ation. A normal polarity ﬁeld direction compatible with the Middle Devonian–Early Carboniferous palaeo-
ﬁeld is therefore resolved from these members. The remaining dyke (5), with a SE trend more comparable to
the Carrock dykes, has a contrasting remanence with similar declination but positive inclination (stereoplot in
Figure 19 and Table 9i). A N to NE ChRM resident in magnetite is also observed in the majority of the dykes
in the Carrock Fell region, including one (site 13) at the summit cutting the granophyre (Figure 19). When
included with results from study of dykes in the same swarm to the northeast (Piper et al., 1978), three sites are
observed to possess shallow inclination ChRMs suggesting that either (i) more than one episode of dyking is
recorded here, or (ii) the E–W dykes have recorded non-dipolar ﬁeld behaviour such as might have occurred
if they were emplaced and magnetized during a reversal of the ancient ﬁeld.
Since all dykes are substantially vertical, no major post-emplacement deformation is apparent at out-
crop and they are adjusted in Table 9 only for the low tilts of Carboniferous strata above the adjoining

Ashgill and mid-Silurian determinations from this study (Sections 4c and 4i). This would therefore be
compatible with an age of emplacement late in the Ordovician igneous episode; however, declinations are
anomolous with respect to all the other Late Ordovician units and are not readily explained as a record of the
geocentric axial dipole ﬁeld.
5. ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION
5a. Lower Palaeozoic apparent polar wander path of the Lake District terrane
Although the granitic rocks associate with batholith emplacement beneath the Lake District inlier are not
ideal for establishing the palaeomagnetic imprint of this event late in the Caledonian Orogeny, a large
number of samples from aureoles and the Shap Granite indicate that the regional geomagnetic ﬁeld was a
shallow dipolar axis directed approximately E–W. This can be compared with a NEÿ=SW ﬁeld axis
identiﬁed from Late Silurian–Early Devonian (‘Old Red Sandstone’) molasse adjoining the Caledonian
orogen and from associated volcanics (Sallomy and Piper, 1973; Torsvik, 1985; Torsvik et al., 1991; Channell
et al., 1992b; Setiabudidaya et al., 1994); in the Welsh Borderlands this palaeoﬁeld is observed to predate
regional Acadian deformation (Channell et al., 1992b). The late Early Devonian–early Middle Devonian
axis recorded in the Lake District terrane, which post-dates all but the late brittle stage of Acadian
deformation, is rotated clockwise by c. 408 and is of shallower inclination; it implies that Britain had rotated
further counterclockwise and moved into equatorial latitudes just south of the equator between Siluro-
Devonian and late Early Devonian times (Table 10). The new data substantiate the westerly loop in the
Siluro-Devonian APW path for Laurasia (Figure 20; Piper and Poppleton, 1990) but enhance its depth.
In the context of the likely volume and concomitant thermal anomaly associated with the regional
batholith (Figure 1), the overprinting identiﬁed in the older Ordovician igneous rocks is remarkably small
and recognized in isolated samples rather than as a ubiquitous partial thermal remanence (PTRM). PTRM
acquisition is a function of both the amplitude and duration of the thermal anomaly (Pullaiah et al., 1975).
Geological evidence from Shap shows that uplift and unrooﬁng following the last Caledonian (Acadian)
tectonic episode was relatively rapid and conﬁned to Devonian times. However, the igneous activity was
associated with ﬁssure metasomatism and low-temperature hydrothermal mineralization along joints and
fractures (e.g. Shap) and along the roof zones of the plutons (Skiddaw (see O’Brien et al., 1985)). Thus
sporadic e ects of late Early Devonian overprinting in the Ordovician rocks is probably attributable to
permeation by these hot solutions.
The new palaeomagnetic results from the Carrock Fell Complex merit close comparison with results from
the adjoining EVG. A positive fold test on components recognized in 27 lavas from stepwise a.f. cleaning and
endpoint analysis (Morris, 1973; Briden and Morris, 1973) indicates that ChRMs in these rocks predate Late
Ordovician F2 folding (Figure 7). Subsequent thermal demagnetization and component analysis has
supported this conclusion (Piper et al., 1997). The ChRM in the EVG succession is therefore pre-Late
Ordovician in age. Faunal evidence suggesting that emplacement of the EVG predated the BVG and
occurred in Early Llanvirn times (Downie and Soper, 1972) has since been revised by Millward and
Molyneux (1992), who show that no such tight constraint is provided by the geological evidence.
Directions of magnetization in the EVG are close to those in the lower part of the BVG and the case for
correlating the two successions is reinforced by the common (normal) polarity found throughout the EVG
and BVG (Piper et al., 1997). The polarity history of Llanvirn and Llandeilo times appears to comprise
frequent reversals and a dominance of reversed polarity (Khramov and Rodionov, 1980; Farr et al., 1993);
in contrast, the lower part of the Caradoc Stage was characterized by uniform normal polarity (Torsvik
and Trench, 1992) embracing the Nemagraptus gracilis and early part of the Diplograptus multidens Bio-
zones (late Llandeilo and early Caradoc). This is the single polarity found throughout 2500 m of EVG and

### page_31
more than 6000 m of the BVG (Piper et al., 1997). Hence palaeomagnetic evidence restores a traditional
correlation between the two groups (Marr, 1900). The palaeomagnetic data imply that all major basic
volcanism in the Lake District, including the intrusive activity at Carrock Fell, Great Cockup and elsewhere,
belongs to a single Late Ordovician episode which followed ﬁnal deposition of the Skiddaw Slates in
Llanvirnian times but was completed by mid-Caradocian times. The normal polarity exhibited by these
igneous events indicates that emplacement of all but the last activity at Carrock Fell (Carrock Granophyre,
Round Knott Dolerite) occurred during the Nemagraptus gracilis–Diplograptus multidens normal-polarity
chron.
Early results from the EVG were not adjusted for plunge of the regional F2 anticline; this omission was
noted by Harris and Dagger (1987) and results are listed in Table 10 following this adjustment. They include
new results (Piper et al., 1997) and are separated on the basis of data from the (lower) Binsey Formation and
(higher) High Ireby Formation; the original study (Briden and Morris, 1973) noted a signiﬁcant di erence
between results from these two formations.
The APW path for this terrane probably commences with the result from the Great Cockup Picrite; the pre-
F2 deformation poles then deﬁne a counterclockwise rotation moving via the EVG poles to the BVG and
Carrock Fell Layered Gabbro poles (Figure 20 and see also Figure 15). The latter result plots between primary
and secondary magnetizations from the BVG; the collective data show an increase in palaeoﬁeld inclination
during the earlier part of Caradoc times which is recognized in primary magnetizations from the BVG (Piper
et al., 1997) and continues to the regional overprint (Channell and McCabe, 1992; Table 10). The path then

### page_32
continues with results from the Carrock Fell Granophyre (CFG2, also corresponding to migration into higher
southerly latitudes, see Table 10), and the pole from the Threlkeld–St John’sMicrogranite with a radiometric
age equivalent to the mid-Ashgill. Thus a ‘hairpin’in the APW path correlates with the Late Ordovician
deformation: poles on the anticlockwise segment are known, or probable, primary poles predating
deformation whilst poles on the clockwise segment post-date deformation.
Continuing motion of this terrane into lower southerly paleolatitudes is recognized between Late Ashgill
and mid-Silurian times (Table 10 and Figure 20). At this stage there seems to be a general accordance of
results across Britain, embracing data from the ‘Younger’granite suites (Torsvik, 1984; Piper, unpublished
data) in the orthotectonic Caledonides in Scotland, to the Lake District (this work and Channell et al.
1993)), and to the border of the Variscan Belt in southern Britain (Torsvik et al., 1993). Declinations are
southerly and inclinations deﬁne shallow southerly paleolatitudes of c. 158S. Terranes now comprising
the British Isles are therefore assumed to have moved into close proximity with the Iapetus Ocean closed,
but with ﬁnal ‘hard’welding of the Laurentian and Avalonian Plates still to be achieved during the Acadian
Episode.
The subsequent APW path from the Lake District terrane moves via the mid-Silurian Howgill Fells pole to
the late Early Devonian poles (Figure 20) and passes via the Late Silurian–Early Devonian poles noted
above and resolved elsewhere in the British Caledonides; it highlights a westerly loop rapidly executed after
mid-Silurian times. As noted elsewhere (Piper et al., 1991; Trench and Torsvik, 1991; Channell et al., 1992b),
the pole had returned to a location close to mid-Silurian position by Middle or Late Devonian times. The
westerly loop was therefore executed between c. 420 and 380 Ma and the hairpin corresponds approximately
to the Acadian deformation.
5b. Comparison with the Welsh Basin: palaeogeography of the Caledonian margin of Avalonia
In Table 10 the summary of Ordovician–Devonian palaeomagnetic results from the Lake District terrane
includes a quality factor (Q) assigned to each pole (Van der Voo, 1993). The Q factor cannot be a deﬁnitive
indicator of the quality of a pole (the pole from the EVG, for example, is a result previously thought to be
tightly constrained to a stratigraphic age), but it does give a good general indication of how satisfactory, or
otherwise, a study is.
Ten Ordovician results with Q 5 3 are now available from the Lake District terrane and seven results with
Q 5 3 cover the Middle–Upper Ordovician interval in the Welsh Basin. In each data set a location for
Eastern Avalonia in intermediate southerly latitudes is recognized, with a motion into higher latitudes in
later Caradocian times. However, there is signiﬁcant contrast in declination (Table 10): whilst in both
terranes the Caradocian declinations are approximately orthogonal to the Upper Ordovician fold axes, in
Wales fold trends are between NNE–SSW and NE–SW whereas in the Lake District trends are approx-
imately E–W. The mean di erence between the declinations of primary Caradocian–early Ashgill
magnetizations in the two regions is 558. This di erence evidently records later relative rotation between
these two blocks (Figure 21). Since Acadian fold trends in both terranes are close to older Upper Ordovician
trends, the rotation probably occurred after the culmination of the Acadian Episode as the Late Precambrian
basement of Eastern Avalonia (the Midland Block (Thorpe et al., 1984) and see Section 2 and Figure 21)
impinged into the orogen prior to onset of horst and graben tectonics during Carboniferous times.
When the two terranes are restored to their Late Ordovician orientation (Figure 21), the Welsh Basin and
Lake District volcanic arcs are seen to have comprised parallel lineaments at the time of their formation.
Geological constraints which need to be incorporated into this reconstruction include the backarc origin of
the Welsh province (Kokelaar, 1988) and the forearc origin of the Lake District province (Millward et al.,
1978). It is also likely that small terranes of greater antiquity such as the Padarn ridge and portions of
Anglesey were sited in between. The combined arc assembly lay along the southern margin of the Iapetus
Ocean; the palaeomagnetic data identify a latitudinal orientation in intermediate southerly latitudes during
the major magmatic activity of Early Caradoc times (Figure 21).
242 J. D. A. PIPER
# 1997 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. GEOLOGICAL JOURNAL, VOL. 32, 211–246 (1997)
 10991034, 1997, 3, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/(SICI)1099-1034(199709)32:3<211::AID-GJ740>3.0.CO;2-O by Curtin University Library, Wiley Online Library on [28/04/2026]. See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License

### page_33
Extinction of the volcanic arc during Ashgill times was followed by ﬂexural deformation and development
of narrow foreland basins as the Laurentian Plate overrode the smaller Avalonian Plate (Kneller, 1991).
These unstable basins were inﬁlled by turbidite deposition between Late Ordovician and Lower Devonian
times. Owing to the paucity of suitable Silurian rocks for palaeomagnetic study, it cannot be positively
conﬁrmed that the conﬁguration of Figure 21 was retained into the Silurian period. However, the Welsh
Silurian Basin (now oriented NNE–SSW to NE–SW) is moved into parallelism with the Windermere Basin
of the Lake District (now oriented approximately E–W) when adjusted for the 558 of relative rotation
indicated by the Late Ordovician data; Acadian fold trends in the two basins are also brought into
parallelism (Figure 22). The two basins are therefore inferred to have retained this conﬁguration during basin
inﬁll and until the climax of Acadian deformation.
A lateral separation was also retained in Silurian times because inﬁlling of the Lake District Basin took
place predominantly by axial input from the east and commenced in Late Ordovician times (Kneller, 1991).
Flexural deformation occurred later behind the arc in Wales because turbidite input commenced here during
Llandovery times and major ﬂexural subsidence was concentrated in late Pridoli and early Devonian times
(King, 1994). Although axial input characterized both early and late stages of inﬁll in both regions, input
into the Welsh Basin was predominantly axial from the west (Figure 22). These input directions are
recognized in both S (sole) structures and in magnetic fabrics of the turbidite units (Allinson, 1991; Piper
et al., 1996). They are brought into alignment following adjustment for the 558 of rotation but highlight the
opposing directions of dominant inﬁll (Figure 22).

of younger cover rocks. The magnetizations indicated are listed in Table 10 and are mostly of Caradocian age but may be as young as
early Ashgill in some of the Welsh examples. (B) Palaeoreconstruction of the north British margin of Eastern Avalonia in Upper
Ordovician and Silurian times adjusted for later rotation between the Welsh Basin and Lake District terrane and incorporating
geological constraints noted in the text
